articles.title: DHS Proposes Ending Deference to Prior H-1B and L-1 Petition Approvals
articles.excerpt: A proposed rule would remove the requirement that USCIS defer to earlier I-129 approvals, exposing H-1B and L-1 extensions and amendments to fresh adjudication, more evidence requests, and higher denial risk.
articles.image_caption: The US Department of Homeland Security headquarters in Washington, DC. DHS has proposed ending automatic deference to prior H-1B and L-1 petition approvals.
articles.nri_angle: Indian nationals are a large share of H-1B holders and file repeated extensions while awaiting green cards, so losing deference to prior approvals would make renewals less predictable for workers and employers.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Iowa City Mother of Four Deported to Sierra Leone Before a Judge Heard Her Case
articles.excerpt: Fatou Traore, in the US for over 20 years and protected from return to Ivory Coast since 2011, was removed to a country she has never visited, advocates say.
articles.image_caption: Downtown Iowa City, Iowa, in a photograph from Wikimedia Commons. Fatou Traore lived in Iowa City for more than 20 years before she was deported on October 13.
articles.nri_angle: A third-country removal carried out despite a 2011 withholding order shows immigrant families why pending protections need active legal confirmation, not assumptions.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.nri_angle: Workers relying on a pending PERM to extend H-1B status beyond six years are the exposed group; approved I-140 holders face limited direct impact.

articles.title: USCIS Narrows Weekend Deadline Rule From October 23: Age Cutoffs Get No Extra Day

articles.nri_angle: Indian H-1B workers and green card applicants with children nearing 21 lose the weekend safety net on age-based filings from October 23.

articles.title: Harvard Law Bars International Students From Externship Clinics Under New Guidance
articles.excerpt: August federal guidance says Curricular Practical Training can be authorised only if the training is required of every student in the programme. Harvard's externships fail that test, closing all 13 clinics to international J.D. students.

articles.title: Federal Agents Search Ilhan Omar's Washington Home Under Court-Authorized Warrant
articles.excerpt: The Justice Department said Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised warrant on October 12 as part of an ongoing investigation. Omar denies wrongdoing, no charges have been reported, and she called the search an attempt to target political enemies.
articles.image_caption: Rep. Ilhan Omar, whose Washington home was searched by federal agents under a court-authorised warrant on October 12.
articles.nri_angle: A federal search of a sitting congresswoman who came to the U.S. as a child refugee signals how immigration enforcement can reach even elected officials, a development immigrant communities are watching closely with no charges filed.

articles.nri_angle: Indian applicants are caught in a UK compliance squeeze: withdrawals of Indian study-visa applications quadrupled to 5.2%, and some universities have added extra screening for Indian applicants.

articles.title: PERM vs H-1B: What the Green-Card Freeze Means for Indian Tech Workers
articles.excerpt: The US has barred eight major tech and IT-services firms, including Microsoft and TCS, from the labor-certification step of the green-card process. Here's how PERM differs from H-1B and what changes for Indian professionals.
articles.image_caption: An editorial illustration shows US President Donald Trump at a podium alongside a US green card and a PERM labor certification form stamped SUSPENDED. The Trump administration has suspended the PERM green-card program for eight major tech firms including Microsoft and TCS, while existing H-1B visas remain unaffected.

articles.title: Federal Court Postpones Rule Ending Duration of Status for Student Visas

articles.image_caption: Students on a US university campus. A federal court has postponed a rule ending duration of status for student visas.
articles.nri_angle: Roughly 352,000 Indian students — the largest international-student cohort in the U.S. — are directly affected: the blocked rule's four-year cap and discretionary extension process would have hit Indian PhD and STEM OPT students hardest.

articles.title: Indian Workers Begin Signing Payout Deals in €31 Million Milan Consulate Settlement
articles.excerpt: Nearly 300 workers, most recruited in India, will receive an average of €50,000 each in back pay and damages after prosecutors found they were paid less than $2 an hour on the U.S. consulate construction site.
articles.image_caption: Scaffolding covers the construction site of the new U.S. Consulate General in Milan, with a worker in an orange vest visible on the structure. Prosecutors found that nearly 300 workers on the project, most recruited in India, were paid less than $2 an hour, and workers have begun signing payout deals under a nearly €31 million settlement.
articles.nri_angle: Most of the exploited workers were recruited in India; the settlement shows how overseas Indian labourers can use host-country legal protections to recover wages and secure residence status.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ontario Calls in Police as College Recruitment Pipeline Under Scrutiny
articles.excerpt: Ontario has referred suspected criminal misuse of student financial aid at private career colleges to provincial police, after inspectors linked student accounts and $219 million in public funds to a network of immigration recruitment firms.
articles.image_caption: An Ontario Provincial Police cruiser. Ontario has referred suspected criminal misuse of student financial aid at private career colleges to the OPP for investigation.
articles.nri_angle: Indian students are the primary market for the recruitment pipeline under scrutiny; families paying lakhs in agent fees face the greatest losses when colleges lose aid eligibility or collapse.

articles.title: Unions and Universities Sue Over USCIS Green Card Rules Targeting Adjustment of Status
articles.excerpt: The federal lawsuit challenges a May policy that treats seeking a green card from inside the US as a negative factor and an August policy letting officers deny applications without requesting more evidence — even for cases filed before the rules existed.
articles.image_caption: Image: @USCIS via X
articles.nri_angle: Indian nationals form the largest employment-based green card cohort with years-long backlogs, making them the likeliest casualties of policies that penalize staying in the US while an application is pending.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

items.text: May 2026 policy treats in-country adjustment negatively.
August 2026 policy allows denials without evidence requests.
Policies apply retroactively to pending applications.
Lawsuit filed by unions and universities.
Indian nationals are the largest group affected.

articles.title: Reported $100,000 OPT Fee Nears Publication, Putting International Students' Work Rights at Risk
articles.excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security's proposed "Optional Practical Training Fees" rule has cleared White House review and could soon be published for public comment — attaching a reported six-figure price tag to the post-graduation work program used by hundreds of thousands of foreign graduates each year.
articles.image_caption: A graphic illustrating the proposed $100,000 fee on the Optional Practical Training program for international graduates. The DHS proposal cleared White House review on September 11, 2026 and now awaits publication in the Federal Register.
articles.nri_angle: With 363,019 Indian students in the US — the largest international student cohort — a six-figure OPT fee would fall hardest on Indian families financing American degrees and the STEM pipeline they feed.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
